about: The words for encounters/rhineland_flanders_793.json: titles, what is seen, what people say, the choices, what comes of each (.out.), and what each card's picture shows (art.<card id>). Written 6 October 2026; a draft for the user to overwrite. Plain wording, no quotation from any modern translation; where a riddle or a rule is put into English the English is ours.

entries.text: The gravel strand under the towered Roman wall at dusk: a big-bellied sunburnt steward in a blue cloak counting sacks aloud down a plank into a small boat, tally sticks in his fist.
Hulls for the king's grain
A big sunburnt man with a bundle of tally sticks is walking down the strand toward your boat, already talking. The king's barley is in the barn at Deutz, and the bread is short on the Scheldt.
A boat! Four men and a dry hold? God sent you. Ten sacks of the king's barley for the landing at Andoverpis, and I pay the carrier in barley.
My Frisian! Not a sack was light last time. I told them so at Deutz. I have ten more for the Scheldt. I always have more.
They say you sold dear somewhere this year. I did not hear it. The clerk heard it. Carry straight this time and he may stop hearing.
The king's barley goes at one penny the measure and not a halfpenny over. Count it out in front of the priest there. He counts as well.
Those are Otbert's sacks from Mogontia, by the knot. Set them down here. I will count them against his list, aloud.
Load the ten sacks for Andoverpis
Ten sacks of barley go down the plank, counted aloud. Wido cuts a tally and breaks it: half for you, half for the ale-wife at Andoverpis.
Hand over the wheat from Mogontia
Eight sacks, counted twice against the Mogontia list. One comes back to you as the carrier's share, with sixteen pennies, and Wido says the count aloud for the whole strand to hear.
Tell him the hold is spoken for
He claps your shoulder as if you had agreed, and goes on down the strand shouting for hulls.
A market on dark trampled earth: a thick-armed man in a leather apron laying a notched measuring stick across a stack of black querns, a Roman wall and one small mast behind.
A hand-breadth either way
A heavy man grey with stone dust sits among stacks of round black stones, a notched stick across his knees. He has two hundred querns roughed out for the English, and the English ports are shut.
The English king asked ours for black stones. Nobody told me what width. Two hundred roughouts, and I do not know where to cut. You cross the sea. Find out.
The man who crosses the sea. I kept a stone back for you. Tell me first what you heard on the Thames.
They say the kings quarrel over a marriage, and ours over the length of English cloaks. A king who measures cloaks will measure millstones next.
The ports are open, they tell me, and I am still guessing. A hand-breadth either way is a boatload wasted.
Lay the measure you were given on his stack
He is a hand-breadth out on every stone, on the side that can still be cut. Six finished pairs go into your hold at no price, and he recuts the whole yard.
Give him a width of your own
He pays thirty pennies for the number and cuts to it. Whether the English mills agree, the first boatload back from the Thames will say; and he will have it stacked where you tie up.
Promise to ask on the Thames
He cuts a notch in his stick for the promise and pats the nearest stone, as a man pats a horse he is not yet selling.
A worn Roman gate arch, one side walled up: a thin stooped clerk on a bench reading from a roll, a merchant before him, and far behind on the strand a tall fair man standing very still.
The names on the list

At the river gate a thin clerk sits in the shade with a wax tablet. In the chest behind him are the king's rolls: every Saxon hostage who has come down the river since the first submission, and in whose keeping.
Name, boat, where from. No, I am not the toll. I keep the lists. A list is the only thing in this town that does not change its story.
Your big Saxon stands on the strand and looks at this gate. If he has a question, the roll of the year of the vow has four hundred answers. I read it for a service.
A woman at the Ruhr mouth counted twelve Weser boys? The roll says twelve. Who is she? No Frank counts that well. I will read you the entry.
The old priest says you carried his people gently. He says a great many things. This one I have written down.
Ask in the old priest's name
He reads the entry aloud, twice: a boy of the Weser, thirteen, given into the keeping of a bishop among the Alemans, sent on by Mogontia. On the strand the mate has stopped breathing.
Carry the bishop's letters to Traiectum for it
He reads the entry and no more, hands you a sealed packet for the bishop's clerk at Traiectum, and writes down that you asked. Your name is on a list now too.
Leave the lists in their chest
He nods and goes back to his tablet. The chest stays shut. The roll will still be there next year; whether the boy is, it does not say.
A Roman cellar lit by a charcoal hearth: a thin clerk holding out a small linen bag with a wax seal on its knot, a balance and a pan of clipped pennies on the table between him and a merchant.
One weight in every market
In the cellar that is the king's mint a clerk reads from a tablet to a man who is arguing about a penny. When the man has gone the clerk turns to you, a small sealed bag in his hand.
The new pennies are to be taken in every place, every town and every market, if they bear the king's name and are full weight. The synod said it. I only say it louder.
The moneyer at Dorestat sent me a penny that is tin under the skin. Test what you are given across the sea. Nick it. Silver is white all the way down.
Thirty pennies I do not trust, and some carry Mogontia's name. Their moneyer should weigh them, not I. Does your boat go up? The seal is mine. I know it.
Take the sealed bag up to Mogontia
The bag goes inside your shirt. He writes your boat on his tablet and, beside it, a small mark that he does not explain.
Pay him to show you the nick and the touchstone
He nicks six pennies in front of you, three good and three not, and makes you find them again by eye. You miss one. He is pleased.
Say the river is long and bags get wet
He puts the bag back in the chest and locks it. He will ask the next boat. He has been asking boats since Easter.

Inside a plain stone church half under scaffolding: a schoolmaster with a rod and six boys on a bench in the light of a west window, a book chest open beside them, a sea-cloaked merchant made to sit at the end of the bench.
The dust of water
In Saint Peter's, under the scaffolding, a master is teaching six boys by the light of the west window. He has seen you looking at the book chest and waves you over without stopping the lesson.
Sit there and be an example. Boys: this man sails to England and back and cannot decline a noun. One of those things is harder. Which?
You carry a letter of the master Alcuin's? On the heathen and Saint Cuthbert's church? Let me copy it before the bishop comes home. I will be quick. I will be careful.
Here is one a boatman can keep. A light dust of water, wet in the sun, dry in the cold, and it will be a river before I am old. Take the Latin with you.
The bishop is at court. He is always at court. The boys think a bishop is a kind of letter that arrives.
Let him copy the York letter
He copies it in an afternoon, reads you every line in your own tongue as he goes, and pays eight pennies for the loan. The riddle goes into your chest on a wax tablet.
Take the riddle and a seat with the boys
You sit through one lesson. The smallest boy corrects you twice. The riddle is yours, in letters you can nearly read.
Say you only came to hear Mass
He shrugs and turns back to the boys. One of them is already drawing your boat on his tablet, with too many oars.

Dusk in a lane of open smithies under a Roman wall: a spare smith with singed eyebrows weighing cut silver on a folding balance, a long bundle in greased wool on the anvil block, hurdles closing the shed behind him.
Iron at dusk

At the quiet end of the smiths' row one shed is closed with hurdles. A spare man with burn-scarred arms is waiting by it as the light goes, a long bundle wrapped in greased wool on the anvil block beside him.
Scythes, knives, boat nails. That is what I sell by day. This is four lengths of iron for a friend at Diusburg, a day down. I weigh, you carry.
You. Good. You did not talk, or I would have heard. Four more for the man on the smith's bench at Diusburg. No coin: coin has a king's face on it.
A blade to a count's man and to no stranger. That is the law. I do not ask a nail which boat it will hold together.
They have forbidden arms to merchants now. They were always forbidden. What is new is that somebody at the Ruhr mouth means it.
Along the keel, stones on top, fleeces on the stones. If a pole goes deep, you never saw me.
Take the bundle for Diusburg
He weighs out sixteen pennies' weight of cut silver, half the fee, without counting twice. Four blades lie along your keel under the ballast. The other half is at Diusburg.
Tell him you carry wine and stones
He nods as if you had refused a cup of ale, and sells you boat nails at a fair price for the rest of his life.
Tell the clerk at the gate what is behind the hurdles
The king's men take the shed apart and find scythes. The clerk has wanted this for five years and eases your toll for two months. The smiths' row goes quiet when you walk down it.

A shelving river bank under a small stone church: a flat barge on rollers with planks off, a wright splitting an oak log with wedges, an empty tar trough, and beyond them a handsome river boat with two small cabins.
Moss and tar
On the bank below Saint Kunibert's a barge lies on rollers with her side planks off. The wright has the bishop's river boat to caulk before the water drops, and an empty tar trough.
The bishop's boat goes down before the feast and I have moss for her and no tar. Three barrels. I pay over the price, and the church pays me, in time.
She has two cabins, this one. A king is to have one and a monk the other. I am told to make her dry. I was not told which cabin matters more.
You again. Is that tar I smell, or only your boat? Set it by the trough.
A flat barge I can sell you by spring. A sea boat, no. We build for the river here. The river is patient; the sea is not.
Take his order for tar
He cuts a tally for three barrels of tar by the end of the season, at a third over the market, and goes back to his wedges.
Sell him a coil of rope from your hold
He tests the lay of it between his thumbs, pays fourteen pennies and hangs it on the barge's stem post.
Watch him split a log, and ask about the river
He tells you where the bar lies below the town this month and which tow-gang drinks. It costs you the time an oak takes to open along the grain.

Families sitting on bundles on a river bank under a high Roman wall, two spearmen, a broad red-faced old priest reading from a small book, a wide plank ferry waiting and a square stone fort on the far shore.
The vow, read again

The bank by the Deutz ferry is full of Saxon households sitting on their bundles under guard, waiting to be moved into Francia. An old red-faced priest is reading to them from a small book, in their own tongue.
I read them the vow again. They say the words. I do not ask what they mean by them. Have you bread to spare, Frisian?
The old and the small ones are to walk to Mogontia. Fourteen days. Your boat could take six of them on the rope. I can pay you in nothing at all.
We had a farm on the Weser. Now a Frank has it. Say the river's name for me once, when you see the sea.
You carried the last ones gently. I heard. It did not make the war better. It made one week of it better.
You took the king's silver for the last boatload. It is lawful. I say Mass for lawful men every day.
Take the old woman and five children upriver for nothing
Six go aboard, light as hens. The priest writes the vow out for you on a leaf, so that you know what they were made to say. The mate rows as if the boat were glass.
Hire the boat to the king's officer instead
Thirty-six pennies, paid on the bank, and the households counted aboard like sacks. It is lawful. The mate does not speak until the piers of Mogontia.
Buy bread for them at the tower and go
Four pennies of bread goes a short way among sixty people. The priest breaks it himself and thanks you by your boat's name.

The round ground floor of a Roman wall tower: a fire on a stone hearth, smoke rising into the hollow dark above, boatmen on benches round the curve of the wall, a tall ale-wife with a ladle and tally sticks on a nail behind her.
The alehouse in the tower
Smoke goes up into the hollow of a Roman wall tower. On the benches round the curve of the wall sit boatmen, a dice cup and a dog; a tall woman with a ladle looks you over once.
Mind the step, my son, the Romans built it for taller men. Ale is a penny the pitcher. Where are you from, and is your boat dry?
There he is. The bench by the fire. Your cup is the one with the chip; I tell the others it is unlucky.
You drank on a stick last time, my son. The stick is behind me on its nail. It has not got shorter.
The river is at my second step. At the third I move the ale upstairs. Do not leave your boat on a short rope tonight.
The potter's widow's son fired two kilns this week and every pot rang. She has no carts to move them. Buy before the other Frisians hear.
They say at Mogontia that I water the ale. Ratburg says it. She has never been further down the river than her own bench.
Pay for the round and listen
Three pennies, and the whole bench tells you what it knows. One thing in it is worth the three pennies, and it is true: the potter's widow has two full kilns to sell and no carts.
Drink on a tally stick
She cuts a stick, splits it and hangs her half on the nail. She will remember. She remembers what you drank the first time.
Settle the old stick
She fits the two halves together, looks at you over them, and throws both in the fire. Your cup comes down off its shelf.

A grey morning among Roman tombs and vegetable plots outside a city wall: six boatmen carrying a body on a plank toward an old oval church of brick, a priest with a wooden cross walking ahead, crows on the tombs.
A grave at the Golden Saints

Outside the north-west corner of the wall, among Roman tombs and cabbage plots, six boatmen are carrying a seventh on a plank. He went under a barge on the tow below the town. The strand has shut its doors for an hour.
Nobody knows where he was from. He hauled on this strand four summers and answered to Long One. The ale-wife has brought his tally stick, to burn it.
He was baptised; I asked. That is all I ask of the drowned. Take a corner of the plank, Frisian. He hauled boats like yours.
The old priest who buried the river's dead for forty years lies there by the wall himself now. I do it as he did: quickly, and by name if there is one.
The soldiers under this floor would not kill at an emperor's order. The river kills without one. Both kinds are buried here.
Take a corner of the plank
The plank is lighter than it should be. Afterwards the tow-gangs on the strand know your boat, and take up its rope a little sooner than the next.
Give twelve pennies for a Mass and the grave
The priest says the Mass by the name the strand gave him. Twelve pennies buys the grave and a board at its head, and nobody on this strand asks you for anything for a year.
Stand at the back with your cap off
It takes as long as three psalms. The crows wait on the Roman tombs. Then the strand opens its doors again and the hammers start.

A market pitch by casks: a tall narrow merchant in dark red holding a green glass beaker up to the light, a chest of bran with more beakers at his feet, and beside him a small wiry woman among stacked grey pots, pointing.
Green glass

On the market's best pitch a tall narrow man sells wine from the cask and, from a chest of bran, green glass beakers to drink it from. The potter's widow on the next pitch is explaining loudly what glass is for.
Taste before you ask the price. No, hold it to the light first. Clay hides a wine. Glass tells you the truth about it.
The widow says glass is for people who want to see what they are cheated of. She is right. That is why honest wine is sold in it.
A monk paid me in a verse once: black, wrinkled, bites the tongue. It goes to the man who can tell me what is born in the furnace and looks like ice.
Born in the furnace, like ice, puts men on the floor: a cup of glass. The Frisian at Mogontia sent you. Then the leaf is yours. I cannot read it either.
Give the answer and take the leaf
He takes a small leaf from the bran at the bottom of the chest, where it has kept dry among the beakers for years. The letters are Latin, and the answer, he says, stings.
Buy a crate of green beakers for the north
Six beakers, packed in bran, not straw. He says a Northman will give for one what a Frank gives for a cask, and for once a seller's word is nearly true.
Taste, praise it, and buy nothing
He rinses the beaker, dries it on his sleeve and hangs it back in its net. The widow next door sells you a clay cup instead, for a handful of news.
A low stone vault under a Roman wall, lamp-lit: casks two deep on oak rails, a boy asleep on the top row, a spare Frisian in a short blue cloak holding a small leaf of parchment at arm's length.
The cask he does not sell
Under the Roman wall a cellar door stands open on casks two deep. A spare Frisian with a tasting cup at his belt is chalking a tally on the door post, and has seen your rope-burned hands.
From Dorestat, by the rope? Then you know what my wine costs before it is wine: weeks of other men's backs.
You came back up. Nobody does that for pleasure. Sit. Mind the boy on the top row; he is asleep, not dead.
Leave silver with me now and two casks lie cellared for you by Martinmas, at the grower's price and my tenth. After Martinmas you pay what the thirsty pay.
Your silver is in the growers' hands and their wine is not yet in mine. Come at Martinmas. I do not sell a promise twice.
A monk left me a leaf for a debt. I cannot read it. He said: answer the one about the cask first. What pours for others and is never drunk itself?
The king says our cloaks are short. He bought them. A short cloak sold is longer than a long one on the shelf.
Answer the cask riddle and ask for the leaf
He nods, goes behind the oldest cask and comes back with a leaf. Born in the furnace, a monk told him it says, and like ice. He sells what goes in it.
Leave ninety pennies for two casks at Martinmas
He weighs the silver, cuts a stick and gives you half. Two casks at the grower's price. He says the price once and does not say it again.
Sit, and drink what he pours
He opens nothing special. It is still better than anything sold at Dorestat. He asks what a cask fetched there at Easter, and listens to the answer twice.

A gravel shore under a Roman wall on a cold bright feast day: casks broached on trestles before timber houses, haulers with cups, a goose on a spit, an ale-wife with a dipper and a Frisian chalking a mark on two casks.
New wine by Martinmas
It is Saint Martin's day. The bishop's church is full, every cask on the Frisians' shore has a spigot in it, and the haulers who brought you up the river are owed their feast.
New wine by Martinmas, new quarrels by Advent. Your bench is kept. A Main man sat on it and I moved him.
Your two casks are on the rails with your mark chalked on them. Grower's price, my tenth. Taste, so that you know I did not swap them.
You left me no silver at the vintage. So today you pay what the thirsty pay. I told you. I told you once.
No bridge to walk out on this year. It burned in May, in the time of three slow psalms. We do not speak of it on a feast.
Roll your two casks down to the boat
Two casks of the new wine, bought at ninety and worth a hundred and twenty here, more at Dorestat, more again over the sea. He walks them to the jetty himself.
Stand the haulers their feast
Eight pennies of new wine and roast goose goes into four haulers and your own crew. Nobody will remember the evening, and everybody will remember who paid.
Hear the feast's Mass at Saint Martin's and go to bed
The bishop's church smells of beeswax and wet wool. You are asleep in the boat before the shore has finished singing, which is the cheapest Martinmas a skipper ever kept.

A long timber hall in grey light: a row of men in borrowed cloaks before a clerk's table of wax tablets, one of them with a scar through his eyebrow turning his head toward a big fair man in the doorway.
Thirty-seven names

Mid-Lent in the bishop's hall. A row of men in borrowed cloaks stands before the clerk's table to be counted. The twenty-ninth has a scar through his left eyebrow, and the mate, in the doorway, has stopped breathing.
Thirty-seven names and their keepers. I am to count them twice. The twenty-ninth has a Frankish name his keeper gave him. I wrote the other beside it: Brunric, of the Weser.
You speak slowly for me. Good. I have not had Saxon in my mouth since I was thirteen. Is she alive? Tell me that first.
I have a wife who has never seen the Weser and a brother who has never seen my wife. Whichever boat I take, I leave kin on a bank.
The bishop can give leave if a man of standing answers for him in silver. A hundred and twenty pennies, returned if the king never calls. Kings call.
Stand surety before the bishop and take him home openly
The bishop writes three lines. Brunric goes down the river in the open, on the mate's bench beside his brother, and nobody may ask for him. His wife follows by cart at the vintage.
Take him aboard after dark and be gone under the piers
The list has thirty-six names at the second counting, or it has thirty-seven and your boat has a guard on it. The clerk sits a long time over the tablet either way.
Carry his word and a lock of his hair, and leave him his vines
He cuts a lock of hair with his vine knife and names the slope where he lives. Tell her the eyebrow healed crooked, he says. The mate says nothing as far as Colonia.
Dusk on a gravel shore: Main boats heaped with sacks, a small round-shouldered clerk striking a wooden measure level, and behind a jetty post a man in a good cloak holding up four fingers.
The king's wheat
Grain boats lie three deep off the mouth of the Main. On the gravel the bishop's clerk is listing hulls; behind a jetty post a man in a good cloak holds up four fingers and looks at the river.
Every hull that will carry the king's wheat to Colonia at the king's price goes on my list. Eight sacks, and one sack in ten to the carrier.
The new measure stands in the hall. Bring yours and have it struck against it. Most find theirs was small. They are always surprised.
Wheat has no memory of whose it was. Half as much again as the clerk's price, for anything set down on my plot after dark.
You are written under the grain men, with a mark. The count at Colonia was whole. I made the mark myself.
A name moved down my list this year. I do not say whose. I say that I can count, and that the ale-wife hears everything.
Go on the list: eight sacks for Colonia
Eight sacks, measured level with a strike in front of you, and a line on the clerk's list. The king's steward will count them off on the strand at Colonia.
Set four sacks down on the dealer's plot after dark
Thirty-six pennies for four sacks, in the dark, by weight. It is the best price of the year. The ale-wife, pouring, did not hear it. She hears everything.
Have your own measure struck against the king's
Yours was small by a thumb's breadth. The clerk burns the bishop's mark into the rim of the corrected one and charges a penny for the lesson.
Watch the measuring, and keep your hold for wine
The clerk strikes each measure level with a stick and says the count aloud. The man behind the jetty post has gone. Your name is on no list, of either kind.

A stone room with one barred window: a thick-set moneyer in a scorched leather apron weighing a penny on a small scale over a cloth, an oak block with a die set in it behind him, a second man with a hammer.
Put it on the cloth
The ring of a hammer comes out into the street a beat late. Inside, a thick-set man with burn-scarred forearms is weighing pennies one by one over a cloth, and does not look up.
Put it on the cloth. All of it. I do not bite coins. I weigh them, which is worse.
Your silver was good last time. I remember silver better than faces.
The new penny is to be taken everywhere. A free man who refuses it pays fifteen shillings. I did not make the rule. I make the penny.
That knot is the Colonia clerk's. He seals a bag as if it held a saint. Give it here. He wants a count; he shall have one he does not like.
Men bring me old pennies and ask if they are still money. They are still silver. That is not the same thing.
Hand over the sealed bag from Colonia
He breaks the seal over the cloth and weighs all thirty. Eleven are light. He taps the table once, writes the count on the bag for Colonia, and pays twenty pennies to a carrier who did not look.
Ask him to teach you the scale and the nick
He shows you once, slowly: the nick, the bend, the ring on stone, the weight against a grain of barley. A man who argues with a scale, he says, should be made to carry one.
Change what foreign silver you have, and do not argue
He takes his tenth and you say nothing. It costs five pennies. He remembers a man who does not argue for longer than he remembers the silver.
Watch one penny struck, and go
One blow. The penny comes off the die bright, with the king's name round it, and goes into a pan with four hundred others exactly like it. That is the point of it.
A builders' yard on a hill above a river bend, lime pits and half-raised church walls: a small clerk at a trestle holding out a book wrapped in waxed linen and tied with an elaborate knot.
A psalter for the Ruhr

On the hill south of the wall the great church is rising round a small old one, and a school recites behind it. The bishop's clerk has a book wrapped in waxed linen on the table, and is looking at your hands.
Liudger the Frisian is building a house of monks up the Ruhr and has nothing to sing from. The school can spare one psalter. It was copied from an English one. I copied it.
A book is the skins of a small herd and a winter of a man's eyes. Wrapped so, laid high, never under a cask. It is worth more than your boat. Forgive me; it is.
You have letters aboard? Then open it once on the way, with clean hands, and see what you are carrying. I should not say that. I say it.
They have made him a bishop. He will need it more now, and have less time to read it.
Take the psalter for the Ruhr mouth
He wraps it a second time and shows you the knot. One book, for the priest Liudger at the Ruhr mouth by Diusburg, who pays on delivery, slowly. The clerk writes your name down. Under books.
Ask him what a book is worth, and to whom
He talks until the bell. A psalter to a priest: thirty pennies and his prayers. To a bishop: a pound. To a heathen: the price of its boards. You could now price one in any market.
Tell him your hold leaks, which is true
He looks relieved, and a little disappointed. A man who says his hold leaks, he says, is the man he would have trusted with it.

The yard of an old stone church patched with Roman brick: a lean grey-tonsured bishop in a dark cloak with lime on its hem, walking fast between two clerks with wax tablets, one hand raised toward a merchant.
Lead for the hill
A lean bishop with lime dust on his hem is crossing the yard of Saint Martin's between two clerks, dictating to both. He stops when he sees a rope-scarred stranger, which is to say a boat.
You came up on the rope from Dorestat? Then you have earned a seat. What do you carry, and whose is it?
You again. A man who comes twice up this river is either honest or stubborn. I can use both.
The queen lies on the hill at Saint Alban's. The king chose the place. I would like a roof over her before I die. Roofs are made of lead.
I sent my old master a comb. He writes that it is a beast with two heads and sixty teeth. A bishop is a beast with one head and sixty petitioners.
The church on the hill is hallowed. Now it wants glass, and wax, and everything a finished thing wants. Nothing is dearer than a finished church.
Take his order for roofing lead
Six pigs of lead for the hill, by the end of the sailing season, at a third over the market. His clerk pays by weight on the day, which is not the custom of bishops.
Sell him a cake of wax from your hold
Forty-eight pennies for a cake of wax, weighed and paid before you have retied the hold. He says the saints burn more than the living eat.
Ask him for three lines to the bishop of Colonia
He writes them standing, on his knee: three lines to Hildebold, the king's chaplain. They will get you past his door-ward. What you say after that is your own affair.
Bow, and let him get on
He is dictating again before you have straightened. One clerk writes lime. The other writes your boat's name, in case.

A long low house with its door to a river: haulers on a bench outside with their feet in a tub, a broad ale-wife in the doorway with a dipper, and one tall silent fair-haired man standing apart with a coil of rope.
Rope hands

A long low house on the Frisians' shore, its door to the river. On the bench outside, haulers sit with their boots off and their feet in a tub. Inside, the ale-wife is pouring and has not stopped talking.
Rope hands. Show me. Yes, you hauled her yourself. First pot is mine to give, for any skipper with his own blisters.
Your bench is kept. A Main man sat on it at Easter and I moved him.
Two haulers want a berth down to the sea. One is a Saxon who will not say where from. He works. I ask no more.
I pull. I row. I do not ask where. Bread, and a place by the mast. I want to see salt water once.
The Main men say the ears upriver stood full and empty both. When grain is thin men sell what they can spare. Wine will be cheap here till the frost.
At Colonia, in that tower, they water the ale and salt the news. Tell Adaltrud I said so. She will pour you a better pot to prove me wrong.
Give the Saxon a berth
Four pennies in his hand and he is aboard before you have finished the pot. He has a little Saxon to teach and no questions to ask. The mate looks at him a long time and moves over.
Pay the score and ask what the Main men say
It is true, as far as two pennies can tell: the growers are selling early and low to buy bread. Wine at Mogontia will be cheap until the frost.
Sit with your feet in the tub and say nothing
The tub is warm. Three tongues argue about the price of a tow. Nobody asks you anything, which on this shore is hospitality.

A Roman gate arch above a river shore: a toll man on a bench under a plank lean-to with a tally stick across his knees, a weathered gang master with a coil of tow rope pointing at a merchant, carts of casks waiting behind.
A day on the rope

Under the river gate the bishop's toll man is hearing a case from his bench, as he does most mornings. The master of the gang that hauled you through the gorge says you owe him a day more than you paid.
The river rose at the rocks and we lay a day under Saint Goar's with the rope in our hands. A day held is a day hauled. Eight pennies.
The custom is: a day lost to the river is the skipper's; a day lost to the gang is the gang's. Who swears the river rose? I want three men who saw it.
You swore here before and the oath did not hold. You may swear again. I will listen with one ear.
You paid without an oath last time. It is remembered, by the gangs most of all.
There is a stick on that nail with your boat's mark on it, from the last time. The gang master asks after it every week. Today we settle both.
Pay the eight pennies
Eight pennies. The gang master spits on them for luck. Next time through the gorge your rope is taken up first, and nobody lies a day under the rocks.
Swear with your crew that the gang lay drunk, not the river high
Three of your men lay their hands on the toll man's relic box. If their oath stands you owe nothing, and the gang has a grudge. If it fails it is double, by the custom.
Ask a man of the shore to speak for you
A householder of the shore says he has known your boat four seasons and the gang master twenty, and leaves it there. The toll man finds for the river. Nobody pays.
Ask for the case to stand over until Martinmas
The toll man cuts a stick for the claim and hangs it up. It costs nothing today. It will be the first thing said to you at this gate when you come again.
A wide brown river crossed by a line of stone piers, each with a bush growing on top: a ferryman leaning on a long pole beside a flat ferry barge, herons on the piers, a low fort on the far bank.
The old piers

Twenty-one stone piers stand in a line across the river to Kastel, brown water piling against each. At the foot of the lane the ferryman is leaning on his pole, looking at them as a man looks at a neighbour's dog.
The king's carpenters are laying oak on the old piers. A bridge is a ferry that does not need feeding. Ten years, they say it will take. I can wait eleven.
There it stands. Carts cross in the time I take to load. People walk out on feast days only to stand on it. I carry what is too drunk to walk.
It burned in three hours and nothing is left above the water. The bishop's men ask who was on the river that night. I was asleep in my sister's loft. Ask her.
The old king meant to build it again in stone. The old king is dead. The piers have stood since the Romans and have not learned to move.
Between the fourth pier and the fifth going down. Never the third. I can tell you why, or I can take you through. One costs more.
Go to the hall and swear what you saw: a fire from the middle, no boat near
The hall writes it down as mischance. The ferry has its trade again, and the ferrymen do not forget whose oath it was. You will not pay for a crossing here while any of them lives.
Pay him three pennies to take you through the piers
He stands in your bow and says nothing until the fifth pier is past. Then he says: that is the only way. You could do it yourself now.
Lean on the rail and let him talk
He talks about the river as of a difficult ox. By the end you know which gravel bar moved at Easter, and what he thinks of kings who measure.
A bare guest-house board in grey spring light: bread, a bowl of beans, leeks and a jug, a monk counting heads with one finger, and a very big fair crewman looking at the beans as at an enemy.
Lenten fare

It is the fast before Easter. At the guest house on Saint Alban's hill the board is set with bread, beans, leeks and thin ale, and the guest-master is counting heads. Your mate is counting what is not on the table.
Bread, beans, leeks. No flesh, no milk, no eggs until the Resurrection. It is the same for the bishop. He complains less than your crew.
The big Saxon of yours looks at my beans as at an enemy. I ask nothing. A priest who asks what a hauler ate in Lent hears things he must then act upon.
At mid-Lent the hostages are brought to the bishop's hall to be counted. They fast too. They have had practice.
Fish is no flesh. The Main is full of it, and the fishermen know what week it is. Their price knows too.
Somebody on the shore smelt bacon from your boat last Lent. I did not write it down. I mention that I could have.
Keep the fast with the house, crew and all
Four days of beans. The crew row as men row on beans. The guest-master writes the boat down among those who kept the fast, which at this house is a list worth being on.
Buy fish for the boat at the Lenten price
Six pennies for what costs two after Easter. It is lawful, it is hot, and the mate eats his share looking at nobody.
Eat with the house, and do not look into the boat after dark
Somebody aboard has a flitch of bacon and a quiet knife. If nobody from the hill walks by the shore tonight, that is the end of it. If somebody does, it is a matter for a priest.

A market inside a Roman gate: sacks of wheat, a tall floury grain merchant with a notched measuring stick, and beside him a blind pilgrim with a staff and a scrip, his face turned toward the sound of the river.
A seat going down
By the sacks of Main wheat in the market a big floury man is talking to a pilgrim with a staff and a white stare. The pilgrim is blind. He wants to pray at the Golden Saints at Colonia before winter.
I take pilgrims down the Main for nothing when the boat is light. It costs me a seat, and God keeps the tally. But my boats stop here. Yours goes on.
I can pay six pennies, or I can pay in psalms. I know all of them. I know which a crew likes in a headwind.
Tell the stone dealer at Colonia the upper mill wants two stones before harvest. That is my freight on your boat, and it weighs nothing.
Give him the seat for nothing
He comes aboard by the feel of the plank and sits where he is put. He sings the crew down the gorge. The grain man tells the bishop's clerk he has a name for him.
Take his six pennies
Six pennies, counted by touch into your palm, each one turned over. He sits in the bow and prays under his breath. It is fair. Nobody says it is more than fair.
Say the boat is full of casks
The grain man shrugs and looks for another hull. The blind man turns his face toward the river, as if he could hear which boat it will be.

Dusk on a mud bank under a green hill: a line of Saxons sitting with bundles and children, two spearmen, a lean steward with tally sticks pointing at a small boat, and a tall crewman standing very still beside it.
Twelve, sitting down
A line of Saxons sits on the mud under the hill with bundles and children, two spearmen over them. The king's steward, tally sticks in his fist, is looking at your boat and counting benches.
A boat. Good. How many can she carry sitting down, and can you leave tomorrow? Twelve to Colonia by the feast. I pay on the day.
You again. You brought back the same number you took. I noticed. I have twelve more. I have always twelve more.
The king gives the order in one breath. I carry it out in forty boats. Count them again at Colonia; they will count them there.
We do not ask where. We ask whether there is bread on the boat, and whether the children may sit in the middle.
The mate has put down his oar. He will not row, he says, in few words and Saxon ones, unless he is told why.
Carry the twelve to Colonia for the king's silver
Thirty-six pennies, paid on the day, and twelve people counted aboard by the steward himself. The children sit in the middle. The mate rows the whole way without a word.
Carry them, and feed them from your own stores
Six pennies of bread and broth out of your own stores, and the same thirty-six from the steward. At Colonia the old priest counts them off, looks at the crumbs in the boat, and then at you.
Tell him the boat is a wine boat
He finds another boat and writes nothing down. The mate picks up his oar. He looks at the road every time the boat lies here.

A smoky timber kitchen: a tall fair woman in an undyed dress with rolled sleeves stirring a great pot, a small wooden cross on a cord at her neck, and in the doorway behind a merchant a very big man who will not come in.
A pot on

The court kitchen is a low hall full of smoke at the top of the hill. A tall fair woman with a wooden cross worn outside her dress is stirring a pot big enough to wash a child in, and does not turn round.
You want bread, you ask the cook. You want something else, say it plainly. I have a pot on.
Gerlind sent you. Then you are the boat with the big Weser man who stands in doors and asks nothing. Tell him to ask.
From the Weser, the year of the vow, they took the sons south by boat. Twelve. To the bishops. Colonia first, then further. One would not answer to the name the priest gave him.
A hostage eats at the king's table and counts the doors. I have counted every band since. Nobody ever brought me the end of a count.
Ask her plainly about a boy of thirteen with a split eyebrow
She puts down the spoon. Twelve boys, by boat, to a bishop among the Alemans; the clerk at Colonia will have the keeper's name. The mate, in the doorway, hears his own river named.
Leave a sack of salt for her kitchen, and ask nothing today
She weighs the sack in one hand and says the steward will think he bought it. Then: come back with your mate. Bring him to the door, and make him open his mouth.
Thank her for the bread and go
She gives you a loaf without being asked, and turns back to the pot. If you see the Weser, she says to the pot, say its name once for me.

A long low smoky alehouse with a fire on the floor: a bargeman on the bench by the door telling a story with both hands, boatmen listening, a stout ale-wife with a dipper watching him with her head on one side.
Said a second time

Under a green bush on a pole: one fire on the floor, boatmen at one end and road people at the other. A bargeman from upriver has the bench by the door and a story, and the ale-wife is watching him tell it.
Sit by the fire end, that is the boat end. You are off the Dorestat boat, are you not? What is bread there?
Your bench is free. I kept your mate's cup; he left it and a knife, and I have only the cup.
Hear it from one who saw. Two salt boats went down at the rocks below Saint Goar's. Salt is three times its price at Mogontia. Sell me yours here, cheap, and save yourself the rope.
The boats coming up from Lippeham say the emperor's great beast lay down there and died. An elephant. Big as a barn, and it died of our weather. That one is true.
Forty came down the road yesterday with their children. Not one spoke. The steward bought every loaf I had.
Your Saxon was looking at the road again. Take him up to the court kitchen. Ask for Hathuswith. Say I sent you.
Sell the boatman a sack of salt at his price
Two pennies for a three-penny sack. At Mogontia, later, salt is what it always was. He tells that story every spring, the ale-wife says, to buy his own salt cheap.
Ask the ale-wife what she thinks of his story
She says, pouring: he owes me for a winter, and no salt boat has sunk at those rocks since my mother's day. Then, lower: take your mate up to the kitchen on the hill. Say I sent you.
Go up to the court kitchen with her name
The path goes up past the barns. The mate walks behind you and says nothing, which for him is consent.
Drink, and keep your salt
The strong ale is not broached till Martinmas. The small ale is honest. The boatman finds another listener before your pot is empty.
Where a smaller river joins a great one: a tall spare tonsured priest in a travel-stained cloak leading a horse toward a flat ferry, a book satchel on his shoulder, alders and a narrow dugout behind.
Books up the Ruhr
At the Ruhr mouth a tall spare priest in a travel-stained cloak is leading his horse down to the ferry, a book satchel on his shoulder. He stops when he sees a Dorestat boat.
You are the Dorestat house with the small boat. I knew your quay before you did. Can she go up a shallow river?
The books came dry. I looked at the bottom of the chest first, forgive me.
I need what a house of prayer needs from nothing: a psalter, a bell, glass for one window. I pay in silver, slowly.
That is the Mogontia clerk's knot. He ties a book as if it might run away. Give it to me. No: first show me your hands.
They have made me bishop at Mimigernaford. I asked to be left with my monks. Nobody heard me.
At York they say the heathen came to the holy island like hornets. I have seen that sky in my sleep.
Hand over the psalter from Mogontia
He opens it at the first psalm and reads standing in the wind. Forty-five pennies now, he says, and the rest in prayers; and Werden will want wax every year while it stands.
Take his order for window glass from Colonia
Glass for one window, before next Martinmas, at a third over the market. He writes it on a wax tablet and loses the stylus in his satchel.
Carry him up to Colonia to be made bishop
He sits amidships with the satchel on his knees and reads the whole way up. At Colonia they will put a ring on him. He asks the crew their names and gets them right.
Ask his blessing on the boat and go
He blesses the boat in Frisian, with a word or two of York in it. God keep her, he says. I will ask at the ferry whether you passed.

The open side of a dark smithy at evening: a bundle of blades without hilts half unwrapped from greased cloth on a bench, a dealer weighing cut silver on a small scale, and outside in the road a spearman looking the other way.
The east road

The smith by the road shoes horses. A man who is not a customer sits on the bench by his door; another, who lodges at the back, has something long wrapped in greased cloth and wants it gone before dinner is over.
You come from the quiet shed at Colonia. Four lengths. Lay them here, under the horse blanket. I weigh; I do not count coin.
Two blades from upriver, unhilted. Silver by weight, not coin. Beyond the Danes' wall a friend gives three times that. I never go there myself. I have a bad knee.
Nothing made of iron goes east without the steward's leave. Not a blade, not a mail shirt. Half goes to the man who finds it. I tell everyone. It saves me walking.
I count who stops at this smith. So far today: you.
You gave us a name here once and took the finder's half. The smiths have not forgotten. Neither have I; it was a good name.
Hand the Colonia bundle to the man at the back
If the man on the bench is looking at the river, the second half of the fee is weighed out and you never met. If he is looking at you, the blades are the king's, and so is your name.
Buy his two blades by weight, for the north

A hundred and ten pennies' weight for two blades worth a hundred and seventy by the law's reckoning, and three times that beyond the Eider. Now they are in your boat, and every toll between here and there has a pole.
Give the dealer's name to the steward for the finder's half
The dealer loses his goods, half to the court and half shared. Your share is paid on the day. No smith between here and Colonia will sell you so much as a boat nail for a year.
Look at the river
The dealer is gone by morning. The smith shoes horses. The man on the bench nods to you next time, which could mean anything.

A gravel spit where a clear brown river meets a grey one: a short, very broad ferryman in a hooded hide cape standing in a flat ferry, driving a pole twice his height into mid-stream, his head tilted to listen.
Iron in the river

Where the Ruhr slides into the Rhine a wide flat ferry lies on a gravel spit. The ferryman, short and very broad, is sounding the mid-stream with a pole twice his height, and has just struck something that rings.
There. Hear it? Iron, long as two men, in his bed. It was old when the Franks came. He keeps it. He lets me knock.
You have the riddle of it. I have the thing. I would not change with you. Mine does not need answering.
Across, or up? Across is a penny for four men. Up her is another matter, and we talk first.
She is running red from the hills. He will be over the lower bank in three days. Move your boat.
The priest pays me a psalm a trip for his books. I have four. The fifth has a hard word in it.
Take the pole and feel the thing for yourself
A bar, with two letters cut in it that he takes for runes. At the alehouse that night a Frisian who has been to England says there is a riddle for exactly this, and says it. It is in your chest now.
Pay him six pennies to show you the Ruhr once, slowly
The bar at the mouth, the snag below Broich, the ford. He shows each once and says its name. After that she is yours to go up, he says, and he will take no second fee.
Watch him work, and keep to the outside of the bend
He is deep there and honest, the ferryman says of the Rhine. He says nothing of the kind about the Ruhr.

A winter dawn from the river: burnt house posts under a hill, long ships drawn up below a new palisade on a wooded height, thin smoke, and across a smaller river the tents and horse lines of a Frankish camp in frost.
The lid on the pot

Burnt house posts under the hill. On the wooded height, a new palisade with long ships drawn up below it; across the Ruhr, the tents and horse lines of the duke's camp in the frost. Both have seen your sail.
You came up past their ships and they let you. Tell me why, and then tell me what is in the boat.
Grain, oats, salt meat, ale. I pay in the emperor's pennies. Sell to the fort and I will hang you from your own mast.
The duke pays in promises. We pay now, in silver that was a church's. Silver has no memory. Bring the sacks to the alder bank after dark.
The grain was dry and the measure was full. My marshal has your silver.
A fort is a pot. I do not need to break it. I need to keep the lid on.
Take the duke's order for oats
Ten sacks of oats for the horse lines, within two months, at half as much again as the market, in the emperor's pennies. The marshal cuts the tally. The duke has already turned to the next thing.
Row four sacks of oats to the alder bank after dark

Forty pennies' weight of broken plate for four sacks of oats, if nobody sees the boat. If a boy carrying sacks talks to the duke's marshal, it is a fine, and a name that nobody at Diusburg will sell a rope to.
Sell to neither, and go upstream
Downstream is theirs until spring, the duke says. You go up. Behind you two smokes stand side by side in the frost, one from each camp, the same colour.
A small bare room in a timber abbey: a book chest with its lid propped open, a round-shouldered canon with a goose quill behind his ear holding a leaf up to the window, chalk dust on his brown tunic.
What ate the words
In a side room of Saint Bavo's a book chest stands with its lid propped open to air. A round-shouldered canon with a quill behind his ear is turning leaves over one by one, looking for holes.
Wipe your hands. No, on your own cloak. Now: can you read, or have you a man aboard who can?
You. Did you guess what ate the words and came away no wiser? Tell me quietly; the boys are listening.
A moth. Yes. It reads more than a canon and is no wiser. I say nothing about the canon. Sit; I will find you a book to look at.
We have eleven books and a chest. The chest is the best of them. It has never been wrong, and nothing has eaten it.
A letter from York went through here, about the heathen and Saint Cuthbert's church. I copied it before it went on. You have it too? Then let me mend my copy from yours.
Take the riddle on a wax tablet
He writes it out small and neat: letters fed me, and I do not know what a letter is. Come back when you have it, he says, and shut the door hard.
Tell him the answer
He is so pleased that he forgets to be fussy. He puts a book in your hands, a real one, and reads you the first page in your own tongue, one finger under the line.
Let him mend his copy of the York letter from yours
He finds four mistakes in his own copy and one, with joy, in yours. Six pennies for the loan, and an hour's talk on what a clean copy is worth to a house with eleven books.
Ask how he keeps the damp out
Juniper smoke, a dry stone, and opening the chest only on a north wind. The damp, he says, is a worse reader than the moth. You could keep a cargo of parchment sound on that advice.
A cellar door on a sand hill above two rivers: a thin tonsured cleric in a patched grey tunic counting wheels of cheese onto a board, tally sticks at his belt, boats and flooded meadows far below.
Counted twice
On the sand hill above the meeting of the rivers, at the cellar door of Saint Peter's, a thin cleric is counting cheeses onto a board and talking to nobody. He goes on counting when he sees you.
You are the one with the small boat. Good. Small boats come when they say. Sit; I will count while we talk.
Back before Saint Bavo's Mass, and the casks not sprung. I had you down for Martinmas. I will change the tally.
Honey was thin two summers running, so wax is dear. A church without candles is a barn. Bring me wax and name a fair price.
The vines on this hill give vinegar. One cask of Rhine wine a year, for the Mass. A Frisian at Mogontia sends it round by Dorestat. He is late.
Before the shearing a fleece is worth a promise. After it, silver. I buy promises. Say nothing of that on the bank.
The new abbot sits at Aachen and reads every tally. A small man. He found four pennies I had not lost yet.
Take his order for wax
Two cakes of wax before the dark days, at a third over the market. He writes it on a tally, reads the tally back to you, and counts the notches.
Take his order for the Mass wine
One cask of Rhenish for the altar, by next Saint Bavo's Mass, at a quarter over. He asks that it come from the Frisian's cellar at Mogontia, and that the staves be counted at both ends.
Count the cheeses with him, aloud
Sixty-one. He had sixty. While he finds the other one he lets slip that the marsh farmers are selling wool ahead of the shearing, cheap, for bread money.

A crowded river bank on an autumn feast day: carts of sacks and cheeses queuing toward a timber abbey with one wooden tower, barges nosed into the clay, benches full outside a long low house, an ale-wife pouring.
Saint Bavo's Mass
The first day of the vintage month: Saint Bavo's Mass. The dues are coming in by cart and barge from as far as the sea, the abbot's men are riding home, and every bench on the bank is taken.
Sit where I can see you. Ale is paid in silver or in news, and news is cheaper if it is true. Today it is silver. Today everybody has news.
I kept your bench. A bargeman from up the Leie has sat on it since, but he did not improve it.
Two rivers, two abbeys, one purse. Guess whose. The carts have been coming since first light, and the cellarer has counted each one twice.
Bavo sold his own people before he was a saint, the book-keeper says. Then he had one of them lead him to prison in chains. Think of it when you price one.
The count's man was counting spears along the bank. When they count spears, hide your sons and sell your ale. My boy is at the wright's yard. A wright's hand is excused.
Hear the Mass at the saint's tomb and leave two pennies
The church is full of tenants in their good cloaks. Two pennies in the dish, a candle, and your boat is named among the day's givers, which half the Scheldt hears.
Sell to the abbot's men before they ride home
Men with a year's dues behind them and a long road ahead buy as men do on a feast. For ten days wine and good cloth fetch more on this bank than at Dorestat.
Take your bench and pay in news
She pours and listens and corrects two of your prices. By dusk you know which bargemen can be hired, which canon is in drink, and when the meadows will flood, by the frogs.
A river bank in thin autumn light: a row of new hulls on blocks, pale and unpainted, chips ankle deep, a pitch pot smoking, and a broad wright with an adze over his shoulder scowling along a plank.
Ships by the dark end of the year

The wrights' strand is ankle deep in chips. A row of keels stands on blocks, more than this bank has ever seen at once, and a broad man with two short fingers is swearing mildly at a plank of green oak.
The emperor wants ships by the dark end of the year. Oak wants three winters. I told the count's man. He wrote down the first part.
Pitch comes out of heathen woods and oak out of Saxon ones. The king fights one and has just done with the other. Guess what both cost.
He came in the dark of the year, looked at my hulls and said nothing. From an emperor, they tell me, that is praise.
You said oak. I have a keel waiting on it and a count's man asking me every day. Where is it?
You sold me oak at the hurry's price. It is in the third hull. I mended your boat exactly as well as you paid me to.
Take his order for oak and pitch
Four loads of oak and two barrels of pitch before the frost, at half as much again as the market. He says the count's man will pay. He says it like a man who has been told so.
Sell him the oak in your hold at the hurry's price
Sixty pennies for a load worth thirty in any other year. He pays, counts the planks twice, and goes back to the keel without another word.
Sell him the oak at the common price
Thirty-six pennies. He looks at you, then at the planks, and nods once. When the emperor walks the row in November your oak is in the second hull, and the wright says so, loudly.
Carry nothing for the fleet
The ships are built anyway, of green oak, and two open their seams in the first winter. He says he told them.

A roofless church in snow, fires burning on its floor: bales and chests stacked where the altar was, a lean fair man weighing a gilt book cover on a small balance, a tonsured captive beside him, long ships on a white bank beyond the broken door.
Sat there a year

The burned abbey has a bank and stakes round it and long ships in a row below. In the roofless church men sit among bales and chests and weigh silver on a folding scale. One of them gives you peace for the length of a bargain.
You came up the river with a hold and no spears. So you are a buyer or a fool. I sell to both.
There are books here with gold on the boards. The boards I can sell anywhere. The leaves only a priest wants, and priests run.
I am of a minster on the Thames. I can write. The book is ours. It begins: In the beginning was the Word. Tell them that at London, if you tell them nothing else.
We are back from Saucourt with fewer men and the same ships. The ships want planks. Have you oak, or only opinions?
The same boat. Then the last silver was good, or you would have stayed away.
Buy the book whole, and the clerk with it
Two hundred pennies by weight, for a gospel book in its boards and a man who can read it. It will cost more than it pays, in silver. The clerk carries the book aboard himself.
Buy plate by weight
A chalice, bent, for half its worth in any market where nobody asks. It is the best bargain of the winter. The people who come back to this bank will know which boat lay at the army's camp.
Buy nothing, and go down by his peace
Say at the river mouth that Ketil gave you peace, he says. It may even help. The clerk watches your boat as far as the bend.

A lean-to in summer light against a big timber house: stag skulls hanging in a row from a rail, a lean fair-haired man in a short Frisian cloak astride a bench sawing a tine, finished combs teeth-up on a board.
Stag heads
Under a lean-to of hurdles, stag skulls hang by their eye-holes from a rail. A lean fair man sits astride a bench with a fine saw, the ground white with dust round his feet, and does not look up.
You have a seaman's hair. Salt and knots. Sit there, out of my light. Did you bring antler?
The same head, a little greyer. Mine too. What did you bring me this time?
A dozen combs for a bundle of stag. It is a bargain for you. It is a better one for me. I do not hide that.
The Danes pay double for a comb with a case. They will not be seen with lice. I respect that in a people.
Your boy has still hands. Leave him with me a summer. I will send back a comb-maker or a boy who hates bone.
This saw is from Colonia, from a man who never asks where his iron goes. For once it goes somewhere honest.
Give a bundle of antler for a dozen combs
He turns every tine over, rejects one, and counts twelve combs off the board, teeth up. The bundle cost you six pennies. The dozen sells for twelve here, and for more with every day's sail north.
Take his order for stag antler
Three bundles before Martinmas, when he goes. Stag, he says: not elk, not ox horn. He can tell with his eyes shut, and will.
Buy a dozen combs for silver
Ten pennies, at the maker's bench, for what is twelve on the bank. He prices everything in combs, and would rather have had antler.
Sit out of his light and watch
Three days to a comb if nobody talks to him. You do not talk. He cuts forty teeth while you watch, and not one is thicker than the next.

A trodden river bank before a big timber house on posts: thin people sitting along its wall with bowls, a large ale-wife with a ladle at the front, a thin priest beside her, and a small boat on the sand point with sacks in her.
Thin ale

On the selling bank nobody is selling grain. Poor people from up river sit along the wall of the big house and are given broth. The ale-wife stands at the front with a ladle and waits to hear what is in your sacks.
No malt to be had above the price of silver. I am brewing thin and saying so. Bring barley and name your own bench.
That is the king's steward's knot, and a week late as ever. Ten sacks. Open them here, where the priest can see the measure.
The grain in the far strips stood tall at Pentecost and there was nothing in the ear. I touched it. I will not say what I thought.
The king's price for barley is two pennies the measure. I have come down from the church to hear whether a skipper can count to two.
You sold dear here once. The stick is by the door, cut deep, where every skipper sees whose mark it is.
You sold at the fair price when you could have had double. I cut no stick for that. Sit down; it is thick today.
Hand over the steward's ten sacks at the king's price

Ten sacks, struck level under the priest's eye. The carrier's share is a barrel of salt pork and fourteen pennies. She breaks the steward's tally and hangs her half on the rafter. That night the ale is thick.
Sell four sacks of your own barley at the king's price
Twelve pennies for four sacks, which is less than they cost you. The herdsmen bring their pigs to your boat's side before they bring them to the bank, and the first thick cup goes to your crew.
Sell four sacks at what a hungry place will bear

It is all sold by the turn of the tide, at seven pennies the sack. She pays, cuts the stick very deep and hangs it by the door. The priest says the feast's prayer for those who sell bread, and looks at nobody.
You have no grain: ask what else would help

Pigs, she says. The herdsmen have nothing to fatten them on and are selling young ones at seven pennies. Pork keeps in salt. Salt is at Walichrum. It is the first clever question a skipper has asked here all year.

A dark little timber church with its west door open on a wide river: two hanging lamps before a plain altar, one unlit, a thin priest in a patched tunic with an iron key on a thong, an iron-hasped chest against the wall.
Peter and Paul

The small timber church on the sand rise has its west door open to the river. Two lamps hang before the altar and one is not lit. The priest names the saint whose day it is before he says good morning.
Peter and Paul keep you. It is their week, the feast of this church. It has a third of what you paid at the toll, so you are already a benefactor. Come in.
You came. The second lamp is still dark. I mention it only because you asked how I was.
A Life of our Willibrord has been written, in good Latin. They have it at Traiectum. I have a chest, thirty pennies, and no book to put in it.
Is that a book in your hold? Under the fleeces? I can smell the boards. Forgive me. What book?
The leaf in my chest curses whoever takes this church's goods: the lot of Judas and the leprosy of Gehazi. The toll man knows it by heart.
Give him the book for his thirty pennies
He holds it open in both hands as if it were hot, and reads the first leaf aloud to an empty church. Then he tells the toll man that the church's third is not to be asked of you again.
Pay for oil for the second lamp
Eight pennies of oil. He lights the second lamp himself and looks up at it with his mouth a little open. Incense and lights, the giver wrote. He did not write who pays for them now.
Stand through the Mass at the back
The church holds thirty and has eleven in it. He says the Mass as if it were three hundred. Afterwards he asks you to greet the schoolmaster at Traiectum, and not to say he asked twice.

A squared oak toll post at the head of a sand point: a short broad toll man holding out a long notched stick in one hand, the other hand open, a thin priest beside him with a wax tablet, both looking at a grounded boat.
The stick and the door
At Michaelmas the toll man's notched stick is laid beside the priest's count of boats, made from the church door. They differ by one. Both men are looking at your boat.
Hand first, talk after. My stick says forty-one boats since Easter. I say it again: forty-one.
From the church door I counted forty-two. The church has a third of the toll. A third of one boat is still the saint's.
One of us has counted this Frisian twice, or one of us has missed him once. You were here at midsummer. Did you pay, and whom?
You swore to your count here before, and it stood. I do not ask you to put your hand out twice.
A man who swears falsely to me loses the hand he swore with. That is the lord king's law, not my joke.
Swear that you paid at the post, once, into his hand
You put your right hand out, flat, and say it. The toll man cuts the stick to forty-two without a word. The priest writes it down. Nobody on this bank has ever lost the hand.
Say only that the saint's third should not be short
The priest's count stands. The toll man pays the saint a third of a boat out of his own purse, looking at you while he does it. He will count your next cargo aloud, twice.
Say you cannot remember one tide from another
They look at each other for the first time that day, and then both at you. The matter is put off to Martinmas, as it is every year.

Inside a big timber house by firelight: a dark-haired young ale-wife with bunches of tally sticks at her belt standing between a skipper and the ale vat, one hand raised, bunches of older sticks hanging from the rafters.
How many sails
The big house on posts has a young ale-wife now, with her grandmother's tally sticks at her belt. She asks every skipper the same thing before she pours, and she is asking you.
You are of the house that had the bench by the post. I have your stick. Sit. How many sails between here and the sea, and whose? Drink after.
Dorestat was plundered at midsummer. A man who swam for it told me at this fire. The count of the island came up and counted our spears. He counted eleven.
Smoke goes up, word goes down river. I trust the smoke.
Tell her plainly: they pass the river mouth every summer, and one flood would bring them here

She does not thank you. She sends the sows inland that week, and the children, and has a pit dug for the priest's chest. When the ships come round the bend on a morning flood, the houses they burn are empty.
Offer to carry her stores and the church's chest inland, for a fee
Twenty pennies for two days' work with the boat in the creeks. The casks, the vat and the chest are a morning's walk inland when the fleet comes. She pays to the penny and cuts a stick for it.
Say the Scheldt is wide and they have richer places to burn
She looks at you as her grandmother looked at a man who had drunk three and said two. In the summer of 836 the Northmen burn the place, and what stands is taken.
